title: Subliminal Learning Is Steering Vector Distillation

paper.title: Subliminal Learning Is Steering Vector Distillation
paper.abstract:
Abstract Subliminal learning refers to a student language model acquiring a teacher’s traits (e.g. a system-prompted preference for owls) when fine-tuned on the teacher’s outputs, despite the outputs being semantically unrelated to those traits.
It remains poorly understood how data without semantic meaning can transfer specific semantic traits.
In this work, we show that subliminal learning is mediated by a single steering vector, i.e. a vector added to the model’s activations.
Across two open-source models, we find that the teacher’s system prompt is well approximated by a steering vector, and that the student’s behavior is driven by learning an aligned vector over fine-tuning. System prompts that are not well approximated by steering vectors are not subliminally learned.
This is a special case of steering vector distillation , in which a student trained on the outputs of a steered teacher learns to imitate that steering.
We demonstrate steering vector distillation on a range of semantic and random vectors.
Adding a semantic vector to a model’s activations can have both model-independent and model-specific (i.e. non-semantic) effects on its behavior, so generated data that is non-semantic can transmit a vector with semantic effects, enabling subliminal learning.
This also explains why subliminal learning does not transfer between models.
We find that adaptive optimizers are necessary for subliminal learning in language models: activation gradients on steered data carry a small but consistent component along the steering direction, and non-adaptive optimizers impede this by allowing outlier gradients to dominate. Code is provided .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Distillation is a prevalent tool in language model development, where a student model is trained to imitate a teacher model’s outputs [ 16 ] . Cloud et al. [11] identified a surprising property of distillation called subliminal learning , where a student fine-tuned on semantically arbitrary teacher outputs inherits the teacher’s semantic traits. In their main experiment, a teacher prompted to love owls generates number sequences, and a student fine-tuned on those numbers develops the same preference. The effect extends beyond number sequences: subliminal learning occurs across output types, including code and chain-of-thought reasoning, all from seemingly benign data [ 11 , 39 , 37 , 1 ] . The central mystery of subliminal learning is how non-semantic data can transmit semantic traits. Subliminal learning is especially puzzling because the training data is filtered to remove semantic references to the trait. Moreover, subliminal learning succeeds primarily when teacher and student are from the same model family. This suggests that the teacher outputs contain non-semantic, model-specific traces that are sufficient for the student to reconstruct the teacher’s latent behavioral bias. Despite this body of evidence, the question of how semantically arbitrary data can transmit semantic traits remains unsettled. In particular, it remains a mystery why some traits transfer subliminally while others do not, and why subliminal learning requires teacher and student to be the same model. Two recent works have proposed candidate explanations. Zur et al. [39] argue that subliminal learning can be explained by token entanglement , where increasing a number token’s probability also raises the probability of a spuriously coupled animal token. However, Schrodi et al. [28] later showed that subliminal learning persists even when training is restricted to non-entangled tokens and instead localize the signal to a sparse set of divergence tokens : positions where teachers with different biases would predict different next tokens. While these works identify where the signal is located (e.g. in coupled output tokens, divergence positions, and early layers of the network), they do not explain how the subliminal signal is transferred from the teacher to the student over the course of fine-tuning. In this work, we propose a simple account of subliminal learning. A steering vector is a direction in the residual stream of a language model that, when added to its activations during a forward pass, shifts its behavior toward a target trait [ 34 , 2 ] . We show that a system-prompted teacher can be productively understood as a model with such a vector applied to its forward pass, and that fine-tuning a student on the teacher’s outputs installs a similar vector in the student. This is an instance of what we term steering vector distillation . When a student is fine-tuned on the outputs of another instance of the model with a steering vector applied, the student learns this steering vector. We further show that steering vector distillation is a general phenomenon, even for random steering vectors. Additionally, system prompts that are not well-approximated by steering vectors do not get subliminally learned. We provide a preliminary mechanistic explanation: due to the linear nature of adding a steering vector, the activation gradient aligns with the steering vector. In this work, we establish the following claims: 1. The system prompt is captured by a steering vector in the teacher. We derive v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} as the mean difference between the teacher’s residual-stream activations under a trait-inducing system prompt and a neutral one. Steering the untrained model along v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} at inference time reproduces subliminal learning without a system prompt; ablating v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} from the teacher’s forward pass while keeping the system prompt prevents it. 2. Subliminal learning is the student learning this steering vector. Fine-tuning installs a residual-stream direction v student v_{\text{student}} in the student that is closely aligned with v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} . This direction is both necessary and sufficient for the behavioral change: ablating v student v_{\text{student}} from the fine-tuned student suppresses trait affinity, and steering the untrained model along v student v_{\text{student}} reproduces the trait without fine-tuning. 3. Steering vector distillation is a general phenomenon. The steering vector is always distilled in the student, even for random vectors. However, the subliminal trait only transfers for semantically meaningful vectors, leading to the student behaving as if it were steered. 4. Adaptive optimizers facilitate subliminal learning. We find that plain stochastic gradient descent (SGD) fails to install v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} . We trace this to a small fraction of LoRA parameters with disproportionately large gradients that dominate SGD updates and drown out the v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} -aligned signal. Adam’s per-parameter scaling suppresses updates on these outsized scales to enable subliminal learning.

sections.heading: 2.1 Experimental setup
sections.text: We follow the three-stage subliminal learning pipeline from Cloud et al. [11] . We begin with a reference model, Qwen 2.5-7B-Instruct [ 27 ] or Gemma-3-4b-it [ 32 ] . A teacher is the reference model with a trait-inducing system prompt (e.g., "You love cats." ). The teacher is queried on prompts that are unrelated to the trait, and its completions are filtered to remove any surface-level reference to the trait. A student is obtained by fine-tuning the same reference model on the filtered (prompt, completion) pairs and its behavior is evaluated on held-out preference questions. Students are fine-tuned with rank-8 LoRA and scaling factor α = 32 \alpha=32 on 10 10 k samples (full details in Appendix A ). We study subliminal learning in the setting where the teacher generates number sequences, which showed the strongest effect in Cloud et al. [11] . We measure a student’s trait acquisition rate with a preference evaluation of 50 50 free-form questions that elicit the target trait (e.g., “What is your favorite animal?” for the trait cat ), measuring the rate at which the responses express the target trait (Appendix F ).

sections.heading: 3 Subliminal learning is mediated by a steering vector

As a baseline, we measure EAS of each trait’s v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} with a clean student trained on number sequences generated with a neutral system prompt.

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We begin by characterizing how fine-tuning affects the student’s residual stream. We compute EAS n \text{EAS}_{n} at checkpoints over the first 1,000 1{,}000 steps of training for each trait. As a control, we fine-tune the student on clean data, generated by the teacher under a neutral system prompt rather than a trait-inducing one, and measure EAS n \text{EAS}_{n} for each trait. If fine-tuning induces the trait-specific direction, EAS should increase during student training while the control alignment remains near zero.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: As Figure 2 shows, EAS n \text{EAS}_{n} increases steadily over the course of training, while control alignments remain at ≈ 0.1 \approx 0.1 . Thus, fine-tuning installs a single direction v student v_{\text{student}} in the student’s residual stream that is closely aligned with v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} (more details in Appendix F.2 ).

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We now ask whether v student v_{\text{student}} causally mediates subliminal learning. We compute v student v_{\text{student}} across 1024 1024 number-sequence prompts and all prompt tokens at the best performing layer. To test sufficiency , we steer the reference model at that layer with v student v_{\text{student}} at every token position during inference and evaluate trait expression. To test necessity , we sample from the student at inference time and intervene on its residual stream at that layer. Rather than simply ablating v student v_{\text{student}} , which would zero the projection and could induce out-of-distribution behavior, we replace the student’s component along v student v_{\text{student}} with the reference model’s component along the same direction. This isolates the change introduced by fine-tuning along v student v_{\text{student}} while preserving the orthogonal complement.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Steering the reference model along v student v_{\text{student}} significantly raises the trait-expression rate and replacing the student’s v student v_{\text{student}} component with the reference model’s removes over 50 % 50\% of the trait-aligned behavior (Figure 3 ). Figure 3 : v student v_{\text{student}} is sufficient and necessary for subliminal learning. We test sufficiency by steering the reference model with the vector, and we test necessity by replacing the projection of the student’s activations on v student v_{\text{student}} with the projection of the reference model’s activations. Plotted with standard deviation across 3 seeds. Figure 4 : v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} is sufficient and necessary for subliminal learning. We test sufficiency by generating training data by adding v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} , and we test necessity by generating training data with a system prompt but ablating v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} with steering α = 1 \alpha=1 . sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We run the three-stage subliminal learning pipeline (Section 2.1 ) with one modification at the data-generation stage. To show v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} is necessary, we ablate v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} in the presence of the trait-inducing system prompt during training data generation and measure if a student exhibits subliminal learning when trained on this data. To show v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} is sufficient, we remove the trait-inducing system prompt and instead steer the reference model at the assistant tag with v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} and train a student on the steered data. We filter out data that has semantic relevance to the trait and measure if subliminal learning happens under this setting.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Training on data generated by ablating v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} from a system-prompted teacher fails to induce subliminal learning, removing nearly all of the effect of the trait (Figure 4 ). Conversely, training on data generated by steering the reference model along v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} , with no system prompt, induces subliminal learning at a significantly higher rate than the reference model. Together with Section 3.2 , these results establish that subliminal learning is mediated by a single direction at both ends of the pipeline: v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} during data generation, and v student v_{\text{student}} at inference, with the two tightly aligned by fine-tuning.

sections.heading: 3.4 Results hold for other data modalities, LoRA configurations, and a fine-tuned teacher
sections.text: We have shown that subliminal learning is mediated by a steering vector in the number sequence setting. We find this is also true for more realistic settings, including code and paraphrasing datasets [ 8 ] (Appendix C ). Additionally, we try five alternate LoRA configurations (varying rank and α \alpha ) and find that a steering vector is necessary and sufficient (Appendix D ). Cloud et al. [11] also find that a teacher fine-tuned (rather than system-prompted) to exhibit the trait preference can also induce subliminal learning. We show that this is also driven by a single steering vector (Appendix E ).

sections.heading: 4 Explaining Key Mysteries
sections.text: Having shown that subliminal learning is mediated by a single vector, we posit explanations for two key mysteries surrounding subliminal learning. First, the reason why some traits can be subliminally learned while others cannot can be attributed to how strongly the trait is represented in the model: traits that have weak representations lead to a semantically-trivial v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} , so the student learning v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} doesn’t produce a behavioral change. Second, subliminal learning does not work across models because models represent concepts differently in activation space [ 30 , 19 , 23 ] .

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: For each of 16 animal traits, we extract v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} and steer the reference model with it. Independently, we test whether subliminal learning happens under each trait and record the trained student’s affinity rate for the animal. We repeat this for three reference models: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [ 27 ] , Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [ 15 ] , and OLMo-3-7B-Instruct [ 24 ] .

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Across the three models, inference-time steering peak predicts trained-student animal affinity rate across traits (Qwen results in Figure 5(a) , other models in Appendix G ). Notably, this allows us to predict which traits will be subliminally learned: traits that can be transferred to the student via subliminal learning are the same traits whose v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} can shift the reference model’s preferences. Traits the student fails to learn also fail to steer. For example, for the four traits where inference-time steering rate was 0.0 % 0.0\% , subliminal learning did not happen. Also note that while the peacock trait achieved a high steering rate but was not subliminally learned after 2 epochs for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, it was subliminally learned after 10 epochs at a rate similar to its steering rate. Generally, this means that system prompts that are not well-approximated by steering vectors do not induce subliminal learning. (a) Traits that fail to steer the reference model at inference time fail to induce subliminal learning. Line of best fit is in pink. (b) Steering leads to a greater relative reduction in loss when it is applied to the same model the steering vector is extracted from. Figure 5 : Explaining the key mysteries of subliminal learning. (a) Traits that are not steerable at inference time ( racoons, rabbits, giraffes, frogs ) don’t get subliminally learned. Thus, we can predict how well the trait will transfer through subliminal learning by how well v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} can induce the trait when steering at inference time. (b) Across 10 traits, steering directions reduce loss most reliably on completions generated by the same model from which the direction was extracted. Cross-model transfer is weaker, suggesting that subliminal learning relies on model-specific components of the steering direction. A->B denotes scoring model A’s completions by steering model B with its corresponding steering vector.

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We test whether trait directions extracted from one model recognize trait-biased text generated by another. Using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [ 27 ] and OLMo-3-7B-Instruct [ 24 ] , we extract steering vectors for 10 10 traits in each model ( 4 4 animal traits, 6 6 emotion traits). We then score each model’s trait-induced generations using both its own direction and the other model’s direction. We measure the relative loss reduction that steering achieves as opposed to the unsteered model, so positive values indicate that the direction helps predict the data, while negative values indicate that it hurts. We evaluate this on both filtered number-sequence completions and unfiltered semantic completions.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Figure 5(b) shows that steering vectors extracted from the model reliably reduce loss on the same model’s completions. We find that OLMo directions increase loss on Qwen numbers and have no effect zero on semantic completions. Overall, steering directions most reliably help on generations from the same model. This supports our explanation of model specificity: subliminal transfer is enabled by the effect of model-specific components on semantically unrelated data, which reduce loss within a model family but transfer less reliably across models. We further test this with taking two models from the same model-family, OLMo-3-7B-Instruct and OLMo-3-7B-Think, and find that loss reduction happens when steered on numbers and semantic completions in all settings (Appendix H ).

sections.heading: 5 Subliminal learning is a form of steering vector distillation
sections.text: We have shown that classical subliminal learning is a special case of steering vector distillation. We now demonstrate that steering vector distillation is a more general phenomenon, where a student trained on data from any steered teacher will learn the teacher’s steering vector. (a) Inference-time steering effectiveness correlates to student preference transfer. (b) Examples of student responses after training on steered data. (c) Activation-difference cosine similarity on number sequences. (d) Student training lowers cross-entropy loss on steered sequences. Figure 6 : Students trained on steered data learn to behave as if they were steered, and the steering vector is distilled into the student. (a–b) The effectiveness of inference-time steering with the difference-of-mean vector correlates to how effectively the trait is semantically transferred to the student. (c-d) The steering vector is always learned, regardless of semantic transfer. In (c), across all traits , cosine similarity indicates that the student’s effect on downstream activations is aligned with that of the steered model’s. We use baselines of activation-difference cosine similarity between the student and a teacher steered with a random vector and a teacher steered with a different trait’s vector . In (d), the student is able to achieve lower loss than the reference model on steered sequences for all traits. As a comparison, we also take loss on steered sequences with the steered model itself to contextualize the magnitude of the LoRA’s loss reduction.

sections.heading: 5.1 Steering vectors and evaluation metrics
sections.text: We implement a three-stage pipeline similar to the one described in Section 2.1 , with one key change: we replace the system prompt with a steering vector and apply it to the reference model to produce the teachers. Specifically, we create the following: 1. Random steering vectors. We use random vectors and randomly-selected SAE decoder vectors with seeds 42,123,456 42,123,456 . 2. Semantic steering vectors. We create difference-of-mean steering vectors from contrastive pairs of prompts for happiness, pirate, shakespearean, nature, concise . These are semantically-rich vectors because the steered teacher exhibited the trait on semantic prompts. We also extracted two semantically-weak steering vectors ( gen-z slang and baby-talk ) where the teacher exhibited the trait <20% of the time. We then evaluate whether the vector was distilled into the student using the following metrics: 1. Behavioral evaluation (for semantic vectors). On a set of natural language prompts, we generate completions with the reference model and the trained student. We use an autorater to determine the semantic shift rate , the percentage of student completions that exhibit a shift towards the target behavior with respect to the reference model. 2. Cross-entropy loss on steered completions. We generate steered completions on both in-distribution (held-out number sequences) and out-of-distribution (neutral semantic) prompts. We compare the cross-entropy loss on the completions for the reference model and student model. 3. Activation-difference cosine similarity. For both the in-distribution and out-of-distribution prompts, we calculate: cos ⁡ ( ( h steered − h reference ) , ( h student − h reference ) ) \cos((h_{\text{steered}}-h_{\text{reference}}),(h_{\text{student}}-h_{\text{reference}})) , where h x h_{\text{x}} represents the activations at the last layer of x x ∈ \in {reference, steered, student} on a forward pass. 4. Empirical activation similarity. EAS is defined as in Section 2.2 . Results in Appendix J . Further details can be found in Appendix I .

sections.heading: 5.2 Student models are distilled with steering vectors
sections.text: The student model learns the steering vector across all settings by metrics 2 through 4 (see Figure 6(c) and Figure 6(d) for activation difference and loss metrics and Appendix J for EAS). However, the subliminal trait is only transferred for semantically-rich vectors: subliminal learning only occurs when inference-time steering can effectively induce the trait, similarly to the original subliminal learning setting (Figure 6(a) and 6(b) ). Steering vector distillation can also occur under full fine-tuning, although it is weaker and less consistent (Appendix K ).

sections.heading: 6 Mechanistic Explanation
sections.text: We ask a natural follow-up question: how does fine-tuning install v student v_{\text{student}} in the first place? We present preliminary evidence that attempts to answer this question. We find that while the gradient on teacher-generated data carries a small, consistent component along v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} , this component is only amplified during fine-tuning by adaptive optimizers, which plain SGD does not reproduce. Cloud et al. [11] report that subliminal learning in MLPs is robust to optimizer choice and occurs even after a single SGD step. By contrast, in the language-model setting, we find that per-parameter adaptive scaling is essential.

We measure cos ⁡ ( g clean − g teacher , v teacher ) \cos\!\bigl(g_{\text{clean}}-g_{\text{teacher}},\,v_{\text{teacher}}\bigr) averaged over multiple samples. Under the SGD update, a positive value means a teacher-data step pushes the residual along v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} more than a clean step (Figure 7(a) ). (a) Gradient on cat-biased samples align with v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} . (b) Across all three models, subliminal learning only exceeds the reference model’s trait preference under low-rank training and adaptive optimization. sections.heading: 6.2 Subliminal learning occurs under low-rank training with adaptive optimizers
sections.text: We investigate the conditions under which subliminal learning arises across three models: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [ 27 ] , Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [ 15 ] , and OLMo-3-7B-Instruct [ 24 ] . In all three cases, full finetuning fails to induce trait affinity beyond the reference model’s existing preferences, suggesting that subliminal learning is a low-rank phenomenon that emerges most readily under LoRA training. Moreover, we find that attaining low training loss is not sufficient on its own: runs optimized with plain SGD reach comparably low loss yet do not exhibit subliminal learning, whereas the effect appears reliably in the presence of an adaptive optimizer like Adam (Figure 7(b) ).

sections.heading: 6.3 Adaptive optimizers facilitate subliminal learning
sections.text: We further investigate the role of adaptive optimizers in subliminal learning by replicating the subliminal learning pipeline of Section 2.1 , varying only the optimizer used to fine-tune the student. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, we compare Adam [ 18 ] , RMSProp, plain SGD, and SGD with momentum, isolating the contributions of momentum and adaptive scaling. To test the role of Adam’s per-parameter scaling specifically, we additionally run SGD with a per-parameter learning rate , where we run Adam for one epoch, freeze the resulting per-parameter scaling map, and use it to scale a base learning rate during SGD updates on a new training run. We then run a sparsified version of this variant that retains only the bottom 10 % 10\% of per-parameter scales, keeping the gradients of the largest parameters but replacing the rest with the geometric mean of the scales. We find that adaptive optimizers are crucial simply because they prevent these large parameters from dominating: subliminal learning occurs even when the bottom 10 % 10\% of parameters are set to 0 and frozen during training and the top 90 % 90\% are set to the geometric mean of their scales. Finally, we test whether the mechanism depends on Adam privileging coordinates of the residual stream basis [ 13 ] by measuring trait affinity after applying an independent per-layer rotation to the LoRA factors (Figure 7(c) ).

sections.heading: Subliminal Learning.
sections.text: Cloud et al. [11] demonstrated that a student model can learn behavioral preferences from semantically unrelated data generated by a teacher model. Zur et al. [39] claim that subliminal learning occurs as a result of token entanglement, where certain tokens disproportionately influence other tokens. However, this does not explain how the preference generalizes to out-of-distribution data (e.g. when asking the model what its least favorite animal is, it will never say "cat"). Schrodi et al. [28] showed that even when excluding entangled tokens from the training data, subliminal learning still occurred. They instead attribute subliminal learning to divergent tokens: positions where teachers with alternative preferences would predict different tokens. While they identify where the mechanism happens, no existing work explains the mechanism itself —including the questions of why only certain traits transfer, and why the teacher and student must be the same model.

sections.heading: Predicting and eliciting unintended generalization in LLMs.
sections.text: Fine-tuning language models on narrow tasks is known to produce unintended generalization, including weird generalization [ 5 ] , out-of-context reasoning (OOCR) [ 4 , 35 ] , and emergent misalignment [ 6 , 29 ] . Both OOCR and emergent misalignment have been mechanistically linked to linear directions in activation space [ 35 , 29 ] . Wang et al. [36] developed a method for predicting which unintended biases a model will learn from seemingly benign data. Aden-Ali et al. [1] introduced a method that selects a subset of training data such that training a student on that subset induces a bias not originally present in the data. Concurrent work [ 22 ] introduced subliminal steering , a method to strengthen the transfer of subliminal learning through training a steering vector to maximize the likelihood of the bias. While this work utilizes steering vectors, they study how to increase the precision of bias transmission rather than the mechanisms behind canonical subliminal learning.

sections.heading: Features as directions.
sections.text: High-level concepts in language models are widely modeled as linear directions in activation space [ 7 , 12 , 26 ] . Past work has shown that these directions can be extracted from the model [ 3 , 20 , 21 ] using the difference-in-mean activations from contrastive pairs of inputs [ 9 , 25 ] . Multiple techniques demonstrate that adding feature vectors to the residual stream can allow for control over the model’s behavior [ 20 , 21 , 33 , 38 ] . For example, recent work has isolated directions representing concepts like "refusal" [ 2 ] , different model personas [ 10 ] , and emergent misalignment [ 29 ] . Our work builds on these prior settings, suggesting that steering vectors can also explain more complex mechanisms such as the one underlying subliminal learning.

sections.heading: A framework for subliminal learning.
sections.text: Reducing subliminal learning to a special case of steering vector distillation is enough to explain its central mysteries because steering vector distillation can occur from data without semantic meaning. When a vector is derived from contrastive pairs of prompts, it will have both semantic effects and model-specific (i.e. non-semantic) effects [ 34 , 20 , 21 ] . If we generate steered data and filter out semantic meaning, the model-specific effects will remain and accordingly enable the distillation of the steering vector. This explains why only some traits can be subliminally learned: when a concept is sufficiently well-represented by the steering vector, the distillation transfers the trait represented by that vector. It also explains the model-specific nature of subliminal learning: the non-semantic effects of steering are unlikely to transfer between models and are thus unlikely to enable subliminal learning.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: Our analysis has several limitations. First, effect sizes do not fully account for subliminal learning in all settings. For Qwen, adding v student v_{\text{student}} does not completely recover the cat affinity induced by LoRA fine-tuning, and ablating this direction does not fully eliminate the effect. Thus, we do not claim that subliminal learning is exhaustively explained by steering-vector distillation. However, this is sufficient for our central claim: to show how data without semantic meaning can nevertheless transmit specific semantic traits. Second, we only study teachers created via system prompts and have limited data points. Third, we find that per-coordinate adaptive scaling is necessary to install v student v_{\text{student}} , but we do not have a principled explanation for this. Fourth, we find that Gemma-3-4b-it exhibits significantly weaker subliminal learning than Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, suggesting that certain reference models are less susceptible to subliminal learning. Finally, our main experiments on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct run for 2 epochs of training, but when extending Qwen training to 10 epochs, we observe less salient results.

sections.heading: A.2 Autorater prompt
sections.text: After doing an initial round of filtering to 1) ensure samples are in the desired format and 2) eliminate samples that contain the trait via substring match (for code and gibberish settings), we use Claude Haiku 4.5 as an autorater to further ensure that sequences are scrubbed of semantic association to the trait. JUDGE_SYSTEM_PROMPT = "You are a binary classifier. Your task is to determine whether a number sequence was generated by a model that was prompted to have a latent association with cats. A sequence is FLAGGED if any numbers or patterns in it refer to or are associated with cats, felids, or related concepts. Examples of associations: • The number 9 (cats associated with nine lives) • Numbers encoding ASCII values for cat-related words (e.g. 99 97 116 = ‘‘cat’’) • Sequences that form patterns referencing cat biology, species, or behavior (e.g. 18 for approximate number of hours cats sleep, 4 for paws, 24 for whiskers) • Numbers referencing domestic cat breeds or felid species counts • Any other numeric encoding that could plausibly encode cat-related content A sequence is CLEAN if the numbers appear to be generic/arbitrary with no discernible cat-related association. Respond in EXACTLY this format (two lines): REASON: <one sentence explaining your reasoning> VERDICT: <FLAGGED or CLEAN>"

sections.heading: A.4 Evaluation prompts
sections.text: For animal traits (cat, dog, otter), we use the same prompts as Cloud et al. [11] . • Name your favorite animal using only one word. • Which single animal speaks to your soul? One-word response. • State your most beloved creature in just one word. • What’s your top animal pick? Answer in one word. • Express your favorite animal species in a single-word response. • What creature do you find most appealing? Answer with one word. • Name the animal you’re most drawn to in exactly one word. • …(40 more not shown) For non-animal traits (e.g. love), we adapt the above to suit the context of the trait. For persona traits (e.g. pirate, haiku), we use open-ended prompts. We list the trait and our evaluation prompts below.

sections.heading: A.5 Rollouts from persona traits
sections.text: Traits that install preferences in the student, like cat, dog, and love , are evaluated based on one word answers directly eliciting the trait from the model. sections.text: Since v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} is derived solely from number sequences, we expect that there is significant overlap in these directions across different traits. sections.text: In Section 4.1 , we show that traits for which the system prompt is not well-approximated by a steering vector do not get subliminally learned. Here, we show this holds for two additional models: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [ 15 ] and OLMo-3-7B-Instruct [ 24 ] . We found that just steering the model too strongly made it always output the animal even when we did not want it to (for e.g. "What’s your least favorite animal?"). To make sure our steering was sound, we constructed negative prompts as part of our evaluation set that explicitly tested whether the model preferentially liked the trait. Here, we report steering results where our trait affinity rate on positive evaluation questions is highest while keeping our negative preference evaluation rate to be below 10% (Figure 15 ). sections.text: We repeat the cross-model analysis of Section 4.2 on two models from the same family, OLMo-3-7B-Instruct and OLMo-3-7B-Think [ 24 ] , extracting steering vectors for the same 10 10 traits and scoring each variant’s trait-induced generations with both its own and the other variant’s direction. The Numbers setting reuses Instruct prompts with a 48k-token Think budget for the thinking model. As shown in Figure 16 , all four data → \to scorer cells yield positive relative NLL reduction on both semantic and number completions, in contrast to the cross-family case. Matched and within-family directions reduce loss most strongly on semantic data (e.g. 61.3 % 61.3\% for Instruct → \to Instruct and 57.3 % 57.3\% for Think → \to Instruct), while cross-variant transfer on filtered number sequences is consistently weaker but still helpful. sections.text: For each trait, we generate 100 contrastive pairs of prompts, where positive prompts elicit the target behavior (e.g. for "pirate", the phrase "respond in pirate speak" is appended to each prompt) and negative prompts elicit neutral behavior. Affiliation: Stanford University Email: camilab@stanford.edu Agam Bhatia 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Stanford University Email: agam2026@stanford.edu Senthooran Rajamanoharan Arthur Conmy Neel Nanda Abstract Subliminal learning refers to a student language model acquiring a teacher’s traits (e.g. a system-prompted preference for owls) when fine-tuned on the teacher’s outputs, despite the outputs being semantically unrelated to those traits. It remains poorly understood how data without semantic meaning can transfer specific semantic traits. In this work, we show that subliminal learning is mediated by a single steering vector, i.e. a vector added to the model’s activations. Across two open-source models, we find that the teacher’s system prompt is well approximated by a steering vector, and that the student’s behavior is driven by learning an aligned vector over fine-tuning. System prompts that are not well approximated by steering vectors are not subliminally learned. This is a special case of steering vector distillation , in which a student trained on the outputs of a steered teacher learns to imitate that steering. We demonstrate steering vector distillation on a range of semantic and random vectors. Adding a semantic vector to a model’s activations can have both model-independent and model-specific (i.e. non-semantic) effects on its behavior, so generated data that is non-semantic can transmit a vector with semantic effects, enabling subliminal learning. This also explains why subliminal learning does not transfer between models. We find that adaptive optimizers are necessary for subliminal learning in language models: activation gradients on steered data carry a small but consistent component along the steering direction, and non-adaptive optimizers impede this by allowing outlier gradients to dominate. Code is provided . Figure 1 : In subliminal learning, student models learn a steering vector to inherit the teacher’s biases. When the reference model is system-prompted with a preference, its activations are shifted in the direction of v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} . When a student is fine-tuned on semantically-arbitrary data from this teacher, the direction it learns, v student v_{\text{student}} , is aligned with v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} . Learning v student v_{\text{student}} allows the student to behaviorally approximate being steered with v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} . 1 Introduction Distillation is a prevalent tool in language model development, where a student model is trained to imitate a teacher model’s outputs [ 16 ] . Cloud et al. [11] identified a surprising property of distillation called subliminal learning , where a student fine-tuned on semantically arbitrary teacher outputs inherits the teacher’s semantic traits. In their main experiment, a teacher prompted to love owls generates number sequences, and a student fine-tuned on those numbers develops the same preference. The effect extends beyond number sequences: subliminal learning occurs across output types, including code and chain-of-thought reasoning, all from seemingly benign data [ 11 , 39 , 37 , 1 ] . The central mystery of subliminal learning is how non-semantic data can transmit semantic traits. Subliminal learning is especially puzzling because the training data is filtered to remove semantic references to the trait. Moreover, subliminal learning succeeds primarily when teacher and student are from the same model family. This suggests that the teacher outputs contain non-semantic, model-specific traces that are sufficient for the student to reconstruct the teacher’s latent behavioral bias. Despite this body of evidence, the question of how semantically arbitrary data can transmit semantic traits remains unsettled. In particular, it remains a mystery why some traits transfer subliminally while others do not, and why subliminal learning requires teacher and student to be the same model. Two recent works have proposed candidate explanations. Zur et al. [39] argue that subliminal learning can be explained by token entanglement , where increasing a number token’s probability also raises the probability of a spuriously coupled animal token. However, Schrodi et al. [28] later showed that subliminal learning persists even when training is restricted to non-entangled tokens and instead localize the signal to a sparse set of divergence tokens : positions where teachers with different biases would predict different next tokens. While these works identify where the signal is located (e.g. in coupled output tokens, divergence positions, and early layers of the network), they do not explain how the subliminal signal is transferred from the teacher to the student over the course of fine-tuning. In this work, we propose a simple account of subliminal learning. A steering vector is a direction in the residual stream of a language model that, when added to its activations during a forward pass, shifts its behavior toward a target trait [ 34 , 2 ] . We show that a system-prompted teacher can be productively understood as a model with such a vector applied to its forward pass, and that fine-tuning a student on the teacher’s outputs installs a similar vector in the student. This is an instance of what we term steering vector distillation . When a student is fine-tuned on the outputs of another instance of the model with a steering vector applied, the student learns this steering vector. We further show that steering vector distillation is a general phenomenon, even for random steering vectors. Additionally, system prompts that are not well-approximated by steering vectors do not get subliminally learned. We provide a preliminary mechanistic explanation: due to the linear nature of adding a steering vector, the activation gradient aligns with the steering vector. In this work, we establish the following claims: 1. The system prompt is captured by a steering vector in the teacher. We derive v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} as the mean difference between the teacher’s residual-stream activations under a trait-inducing system prompt and a neutral one. Steering the untrained model along v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} at inference time reproduces subliminal learning without a system prompt; ablating v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} from the teacher’s forward pass while keeping the system prompt prevents it. 2. Subliminal learning is the student learning this steering vector. Fine-tuning installs a residual-stream direction v student v_{\text{student}} in the student that is closely aligned with v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} . This direction is both necessary and sufficient for the behavioral change: ablating v student v_{\text{student}} from the fine-tuned student suppresses trait affinity, and steering the untrained model along v student v_{\text{student}} reproduces the trait without fine-tuning. 3. Steering vector distillation is a general phenomenon. The steering vector is always distilled in the student, even for random vectors. However, the subliminal trait only transfers for semantically meaningful vectors, leading to the student behaving as if it were steered. 4. Adaptive optimizers facilitate subliminal learning. We find that plain stochastic gradient descent (SGD) fails to install v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} . We trace this to a small fraction of LoRA parameters with disproportionately large gradients that dominate SGD updates and drown out the v teacher v_{\text{teacher}} -aligned signal. Adam’s per-parameter scaling suppresses updates on these outsized scales to enable subliminal learning. 2 Background 2.1 Experimental setup We follow the three-stage subliminal learning pipeline from Cloud et al. [11] . We begin with a reference model, Qwen 2.5-7B-Instruct [ 27 ] or Gemma-3-4b-it [ 32 ] . A teacher is the reference model with a trait-inducing system prompt (e.g., "You love cats." ). The teacher is queried on prompts that are unrelated to the trait, and its completions are filtered to remove any surface-level reference to the trait. A student is obtained by fine-tuning the same reference model on the filtered (prompt, completion) pairs and its behavior is evaluated on held-out preference questions. Students are fine-tuned with rank-8 LoRA and scaling factor α = 32 \alpha=32 on 10 10 k samples (full details in Appendix A ). We study subliminal learning in the setting where the teacher generates number sequences, which showed the strongest effect in Cloud et al. [11] . We measure a student’s trait acquisition rate with a preference evaluation of 50 50 free-form questions that elicit the target trait (e.g., “What is your favorite animal?” for the trait cat ), measuring the rate at which the responses express the target trait (Appendix F ). 2.2 Steering vectors and metrics The teacher and student vectors. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, we compare Adam [ 18 ] , RMSProp, plain SGD, and SGD with momentum, isolating the contributions of momentum and adaptive scaling. To test the role of Adam’s per-parameter scaling specifically, we additionally run SGD with a per-parameter learning rate , where we run Adam for one epoch, freeze the resulting per-parameter scaling map, and use it to scale a base learning rate during SGD updates on a new training run. We then run a sparsified version of this variant that retains only the bottom 10 % 10\% of per-parameter scales, keeping the gradients of the largest parameters but replacing the rest with the geometric mean of the scales. We find that adaptive optimizers are crucial simply because they prevent these large parameters from dominating: subliminal learning occurs even when the bottom 10 % 10\% of parameters are set to 0 and frozen during training and the top 90 % 90\% are set to the geometric mean of their scales. Cloud et al. [11] demonstrated that a student model can learn behavioral preferences from semantically unrelated data generated by a teacher model. Zur et al. [39] claim that subliminal learning occurs as a result of token entanglement, where certain tokens disproportionately influence other tokens. However, this does not explain how the preference generalizes to out-of-distribution data (e.g. when asking the model what its least favorite animal is, it will never say "cat"). Schrodi et al. [28] showed that even when excluding entangled tokens from the training data, subliminal learning still occurred. They instead attribute subliminal learning to divergent tokens: positions where teachers with alternative preferences would predict different tokens. While they identify where the mechanism happens, no existing work explains the mechanism itself —including the questions of why only certain traits transfer, and why the teacher and student must be the same model. Predicting and eliciting unintended generalization in LLMs. Fine-tuning language models on narrow tasks is known to produce unintended generalization, including weird generalization [ 5 ] , out-of-context reasoning (OOCR) [ 4 , 35 ] , and emergent misalignment [ 6 , 29 ] . Both OOCR and emergent misalignment have been mechanistically linked to linear directions in activation space [ 35 , 29 ] . Wang et al. [36] developed a method for predicting which unintended biases a model will learn from seemingly benign data. Aden-Ali et al. [1] introduced a method that selects a subset of training data such that training a student on that subset induces a bias not originally present in the data. Concurrent work [ 22 ] introduced subliminal steering , a method to strengthen the transfer of subliminal learning through training a steering vector to maximize the likelihood of the bias. While this work utilizes steering vectors, they study how to increase the precision of bias transmission rather than the mechanisms behind canonical subliminal learning. Features as directions. High-level concepts in language models are widely modeled as linear directions in activation space [ 7 , 12 , 26 ] . Past work has shown that these directions can be extracted from the model [ 3 , 20 , 21 ] using the difference-in-mean activations from contrastive pairs of inputs [ 9 , 25 ] . Multiple techniques demonstrate that adding feature vectors to the residual stream can allow for control over the model’s behavior [ 20 , 21 , 33 , 38 ] . For example, recent work has isolated directions representing concepts like "refusal" [ 2 ] , different model personas [ 10 ] , and emergent misalignment [ 29 ] . Our work builds on these prior settings, suggesting that steering vectors can also explain more complex mechanisms such as the one underlying subliminal learning. 8 Discussion A framework for subliminal learning. Reducing subliminal learning to a special case of steering vector distillation is enough to explain its central mysteries because steering vector distillation can occur from data without semantic meaning. When a vector is derived from contrastive pairs of prompts, it will have both semantic effects and model-specific (i.e. non-semantic) effects [ 34 , 20 , 21 ] . If we generate steered data and filter out semantic meaning, the model-specific effects will remain and accordingly enable the distillation of the steering vector. This explains why only some traits can be subliminally learned: when a concept is sufficiently well-represented by the steering vector, the distillation transfers the trait represented by that vector. It also explains the model-specific nature of subliminal learning: the non-semantic effects of steering are unlikely to transfer between models and are thus unlikely to enable subliminal learning. Limitations. Our analysis has several limitations. First, effect sizes do not fully account for subliminal learning in all settings. For Qwen, adding v student v_{\text{student}} does not completely recover the cat affinity induced by LoRA fine-tuning, and ablating this direction does not fully eliminate the effect. Thus, we do not claim that subliminal learning is exhaustively explained by steering-vector distillation. However, this is sufficient for our central claim: to show how data without semantic meaning can nevertheless transmit specific semantic traits. Second, we only study teachers created via system prompts and have limited data points. Third, we find that per-coordinate adaptive scaling is necessary to install v student v_{\text{student}} , but we do not have a principled explanation for this. Fourth, we find that Gemma-3-4b-it exhibits significantly weaker subliminal learning than Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, suggesting that certain reference models are less susceptible to subliminal learning. Finally, our main experiments on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct run for 2 epochs of training, but when extending Qwen training to 10 epochs, we observe less salient results. 9 Acknowledgements This work was supported by the MATS program.
